chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Sawwar, from Al-Hasan, who said:

Indeed, when Ali (peace be upon him) defeated Talha and Al-Zubayr, the people came back in defeat, so they passed by a pregnant woman on the road. She panicked from them, so she cast out what was in her belly alive. It was restless until it died, then its mother died after it.

So Ali (peace be upon him) and his companions passed by her, and she was lying there with her child on the road. He asked them about her matter, so they said to him, 'She was pregnant, so she panicked when she saw the fighting and the defeat.'
He said, 'So he asked them, which of the two died before its companion?' So they said, 'Her son died before her.'
He said, 'So he called for her husband, the father of the deceased boy, so he made him inherit two-thirds of the wergild from his son, and he made the mother inherit one-third of the wergild.'

Then he made the husband inherit from his deceased wife half of the one-third of the wergild which she had inherited from her deceased son, and he made the relatives of the deceased inherit the remainder.

He said, 'Then he made the husband inherit also from the wergild of the deceased wife, half the wergild, and it was two thousand and five hundred dirhams, and that is because there was no child for her except the one she cast out when she panicked.'
He said, 'And he paid all of that from the treasury of Basra.'

key_terms.الدِّيَة: Blood money or compensation paid for death or injury

ai.seo_question: How is blood money distributed when a pregnant woman and her unborn child both die in an incident?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* illustrates Imam Ali’s (AS) application of inheritance law in a complex case of simultaneous death (*mawt al-shakk*), where the order of demise was unknown. It highlights the Shia scholarly principle that when the sequence of death cannot be determined, the shares are distributed based on the presumption that the mother and child were distinct legal entities, allowing the husband to inherit from both the mother’s share and the child’s share. This ruling underscores the precision of early Islamic jurisprudence in handling ambiguous causality in blood money (*diyah*) distribution.
